21081-scientific-american-volume-xliii-n:
Dated December 18, 1880, this weekly issue of Scientific American calls itself a journal of practical information, art, science, mechanics, chemistry, and manufactures. It was published in New York and cost $3.20 a year, postage prepaid. One issue shows what curious readers wanted each week.

Contents range over a new air engine, a hand-power band saw, a submarine gun, and the eruption of Mauna Loa. Shorter notes answer questions on batteries, belts, carbons, and tempering chisels. Pieces on business colleges, the Hercules beetle, and the harbour at Montreal sit side by side. It is a snapshot of invention in 1880.
21899-a-rip-van-winkle-of-the-kalahari-a:
Seven tales of South-West Africa fill Frederick Carruthers Cornell's A Rip Van Winkle of the Kalahari, published at Cape Town and London. The title story begins with a trader who crossed the Kunene River into Amboland after elephants and ivory. In German territory, where roads were few and much land unexplored, he meets a man with a wild tale. Sleep, pleasant berries, and an awakening forty years later give the story its Rip Van Winkle turn.

Other tales salt the great north-eastern fields with a prospector named Dick Sydney, walk the path of skulls, and drink the waters of Erongo. Cornell knew the desert country at first hand. His Africa is sandstorms, pans, poison flowers, and craters. The stories mix fact, yarn, and wonder in a prospector's voice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-de-troke:
John de Trokelowe was a Benedictine chronicler of St. Albans whose annals cover the reigns of Edward I and Edward II. A monk of St. Albans living at the dependent priory of Tynemouth in 1294, he was caught in the priory's bid for independence and sent back to St. Albans as a prisoner by Abbot John of Berkamsted.

There he wrote his Annals from 1259 to 1296 and a useful account of Edward II's reign from 1307 to 1323, after which Henry de Blaneford continued the chronicle. A reference to the execution of Mortimer shows he was still writing after 1330, though his birth and death dates are unknown. His work, edited by Riley in the Rolls Series, remains a valuable monastic record of troubled years in church and kingdom.

doe-osti-3412942-entanglement-informed-t: Quantum computers come in different flavors — adiabatic machines and gate-based optimizers among them. Quiroz and Titum develop entanglement-informed translations between AQC and QAOA, mapping problems from one style to the other. The translations let researchers pick the right quantum tool for each job.
elissa-or-the-doom-of-zimbabwe:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this novella to rebuild the lost Phoenician city behind the ruins of Great Zimbabwe in Rhodesia. His note in the text admits the evidence is scant: old workings, vast walls, and temples to Phoenician gods. The story he builds on them is headed by Elissa, priestess of the Baaltis, the goddess of the city.

Prince Aziel, a Jewish prince come with a trading caravan, plights his troth where the city's faith forbids it. King Ithobal, the prophet Issachar, and the merchant Metem fill out the court. Sacrilege, martyrdom, sanctuary, and the cage of death mark the chapters as the surrounding tribes close in. Haggard first printed the tale in his 1900 volume Black Heart and White Heart, and Other Stories; this hosted text keeps that volume's dedication and author's note.
govdocs-archive_org-montauk-the-alien-co:
Montauk: The Alien Connection tells the story of Stewart Swerdlow, a man who said his extrasensory abilities drew him into secret government work. It belongs to the Montauk literature, the body of claims that grew up around alleged experiments at Montauk, Long Island.

Swerdlow describes being watched and used for his mental gifts, then deprogrammed with the help of Preston Nichols, a central figure in the Montauk stories. He also tells of being jailed after refusing to cut his ties with Nichols. The book is presented as an archive holding, a first-person account at the heart of the Montauk myth.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FrazierBuellWes:
A manuscript titled The Bag, most likely by Harold Weisberg, takes up the paper bag in the Kennedy case and Buell Wesley Frazier. Frazier was the young man who drove Lee Harvey Oswald to work on the morning of the assassination. The bag was the package Oswald was said to have carried that day.

Few objects in the case carry more argument per ounce. Whether the bag held a rifle, and how it was handled, shaped the case against Oswald. A manuscript devoted to it shows Weisberg's method: one piece of evidence, examined until it gives up its problems.
lucan-pharsalia-rowe:
Lucan, a young Roman poet under Nero, wrote the Pharsalia on Caesar's civil war. Nicholas Rowe's translation presents the unfinished epic in English couplets. Lucan died by Nero's order at twenty-five, leaving ten books.

The poem follows Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon and Pompey's fall. Cato becomes its moral hero, dying nobly rather than submitting to tyranny. Lucan drops the gods and fills the space with rhetoric and horror. Witches, deserts, and sea battles crowd his verses. Rowe, himself a playwright, drives the story forward energetically. The epic reads Rome's tragedy as the death of liberty itself.
podcast-joerogan-EhU-yzauNWE:
Harvard astronomer Avi Loeb joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1596. Loeb made headlines by arguing that an interstellar object that passed our system might be alien technology. Most of his peers disagreed, which is exactly why his case draws a crowd.

He explains the object's odd path and shine, and why he thinks a natural rock does not fit. Rogan asks about the pushback Loeb took from other scientists and his project to hunt for more such visitors. The episode is a famous scientist's heresy stated calmly, and a lesson in how science fights over its edges.
podcast-tuckercarlson-3Wi_zQX--wE:
An economist joins Tucker Carlson to advance a sweeping thesis: every major war begins under false pretenses, and central banks stand behind the pattern. The guest walks through the claim war by war, arguing that the stated causes of conflicts rarely match the financial interests that profit from them.

Carlson, long skeptical of American wars, presses for the mechanism: who lends, who gains, and how the story sold to the public gets built. The argument echoes an old tradition of war criticism that runs through American history. Listeners get the strongest version of it here, from a guest who treats banking as the hidden constant of modern conflict. The episode is kept as the argument was made, for audiences to test against the record.
the-dog-crusoe-and-his-master-a-story-of:
Robert Michael Ballantyne's The Dog Crusoe and His Master, subtitled A Story of Adventure in the Western Prairies, is dated 1894. Its contents run from Crusoe's puppyhood and a shooting match to his training and a mission of peace. The title page lists Ballantyne's other boys' books, among them The Coral Island, Ungava, and Martin Rattler.

Dick, the young master, and Crusoe cross the plains on hunts and errands among Native peoples and traders. Ballantyne packs the tale with camp craft and close calls. It stands as a prime case of Victorian boys' adventure writing.
